A TRS R is said to be a homeomorphic embedding if for any l → r in R, l ⊵emb r. ▶ Definition 27 (Graph Embedded TRS [24]). Consider the following reduction relation, ∗ − →Rgemb , where Rgemb is the set of rewrite rules given by the instantiation of the following rule schema: for any f ∈ Σ: (1) f (x1 , . . . , xn ) → xi , (2) f (x1 , . . . , xi−1 , xi , xi+1 , . . . , xn ) → f (x1 , . . . , xi−1 , xi+1 , . . . , xn ), and for any f, g ∈ Σ: (3) f (x1 , . . . , xi−1 , g(z), xi+1 , . . . , xm ) → g(x1 , . . . , xi−1 , z, xi+1 , . . . , xm ), (4) f (x1 , . . . , xi−1 , g(z), xi+1 , . . . , xm ) → f (x1 , . . . , xi−1 , z, xi+1 , . . . , xm ). We say a term t′ is graph-embedded in a term t, denoted t ⪰gemb t′ , if t′ is a well-formed ∗ term and there exists a term s such that t − →Rgemb s ≈ t′ . A TRS R is graph-embedded if for any l → r ∈ R, l ⪰ r or r is a constant. Note that in the definition above, rules in Rgemb ignore function arities, so intermediate terms between t and t′ may be ill-formed. Only the final term t′ must satisfy standard well-formedness conditions on arities and variable occurrences. Every homeomorphic-embedding class is strictly contained in the graph-embedded class. However, deduction remains undecidable in both classes, as shown in Figure 1. In contrast, contracting TRSs form a restricted fragment of these classes for which knowledge problems become decidable. ▶ Definition 28 (Subterm Permutation and Leaf Permutation [9]). We define two types of permutations ≈s and ≈l : 1. For terms t and t′ , we say t is subterm permutatively equal to t′ , denoted t ≈s t′ , if one of the following holds: a. t = t′ , where t and t′ are constants or variables, or b. t = f (u1 , . . . , un ) and t′ = f (uσ(1) , . . . , uσ(n) ), where f is an n-ary function symbol, n ≥ 1, and σ is a permutation of the indices (1, . . . , n). 2. For terms t and t′ , we say t is leaf permutatively equal to t′ , denoted t ≈l t′ , if t′ is obtained from t via a permutation of variables and constants occurring in t.

context: ▶ Lemma 39. Given a weight function w : Σ∪N → N>0 and a w-measure φ : T (Σ, V ∪N ) → N>0 . Let E be a VBFD theory. For each equation l ≈ r ∈ E, there exists a positive constant cl≈r > 0 such that for every substitution σ, φ(lσ)−φ(rσ) = cl≈r . Moreover, φ(s)−φ(t) = cl≈r if s and t are terms satisfying s →E t by using rule l → r ∈ E. This class is quite restrictive. In particular, any function symbol occurring on the righthand side of an axiom must also occur on the left-hand side. Because variable occurrences are preserved while the total number of function symbols decreases, the left-hand side must contain constants, some of which necessarily disappear or decrease in number on the right-hand side. We conjecture that deduction and static equivalence is decidable for VBFD equational theories. ▶ Conjecture 40. Deduction is decidable for VBFD equational theories. ▶ Conjecture 41. Static equivalence is undecidable for VBFD equational theories.

context: These problems are known as knowledge problems in the analysis of security protocols. For an equational theory E, the relationship between deduction and static equivalence is delicate: there are theories where deduction is decidable but static equivalence is undecidable [8], and deduction itself may be undecidable [1]. Conversely, decidability of static equivalence implies decidability of deduction, but only via an extension of the signature with a fresh uninterpreted symbol. Thus it remains open whether static equivalence is inherently harder than deduction in the general setting, without such extensions. These knowledge problems are also closely related to classical term rewriting problems such as unification and matching; see [19] for a detailed account. 3 Structurally Balanced Rewrite Rules In this section, we review both classical and recent results concerning equations in which the occurrences of symbols are, in some sense, preserved from left to right. We begin with a review of the most general classes, the permutative and leaf-permutative classes, in Section 3.1. The decidability problems for these classes have been extensively studied in [18]. Section 3.2 presents our new contributions in refining the permutative classes. 3.1 Revisiting Permutative TRS We discuss here some known results on permutative classes and its restrictions. These classes and their restrictions have been extensively studied not only in the context of knowledge problems, but also more broadly, for example in connection with unification problems in term rewriting.
